bodies.name: Sun
facts: Contains 99.86% of the mass in the entire solar system.
Surface (photosphere) temperature is about 5,500°C; the core reaches ~15 million °C.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.

bodies.name: Mercury
facts: Smallest planet in the solar system, only slightly bigger than the Moon.
A day on Mercury (sunrise to sunrise) lasts 176 Earth days — longer than its year.
Temperatures swing from 430°C in sunlight to -180°C at night with no atmosphere to trap heat.

bodies.name: Venus
facts: Hottest planet in the solar system due to a runaway greenhouse effect from its thick CO2 atmosphere.
Rotates backwards (retrograde) and so slowly that its day is longer than its year.
Surface pressure is 92x Earth's — like being 900m deep in Earth's ocean.

bodies.name: Earth
facts: The only known planet with liquid water on its surface and confirmed life.
71% of the surface is covered by ocean.
Its axial tilt of 23.44° is what causes the seasons.

bodies.name: Moon
facts: Tidally locked to Earth — the same side always faces us.
Formed roughly 4.5 billion years ago, likely from debris after a Mars-sized body struck early Earth.
Slowly drifting away from Earth at about 3.8 cm per year.

bodies.name: Mars
facts: Home to Olympus Mons, the largest volcano in the solar system (~22km tall).
Its red color comes from iron oxide (rust) covering the surface.
Has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, likely captured asteroids.

bodies.name: Jupiter
facts: Largest planet — more massive than all other planets combined.
The Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth that has raged for centuries.
Spins so fast (9.9-hour day) that it visibly bulges at the equator.

bodies.name: Saturn
facts: Its rings are made almost entirely of water ice, ranging from dust grains to boulder-sized chunks.
Least dense planet in the solar system — it would float in water if there were an ocean big enough.
Has 146 confirmed moons, more than any other planet.

bodies.name: Uranus
facts: Rotates almost entirely on its side, likely from an ancient massive collision.
Its faint rings were only discovered in 1977.
Coldest planetary atmosphere in the solar system despite not being the farthest from the Sun.

bodies.name: Neptune
facts: Has the fastest winds in the solar system, clocked over 2,100 km/h.
Takes 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun — it has only completed one orbit since its discovery in 1846.
Discovered by mathematical prediction before it was ever directly observed.

bodies.name: Phobos
facts: Orbits Mars in just 7.66 hours — faster than Mars itself rotates, so it rises in the west and sets in the east.
Only 9,376 km from Mars's center, closer than any other moon is to its planet in the solar system.
Spiraling inward by about 2cm a year; will likely be torn apart by tidal forces or crash into Mars in ~30-50 million years.

bodies.name: Deimos
facts: The smaller and outer of Mars's two moons, likely a captured asteroid.
So small and low-gravity that a rock dropped from your hand would take almost 10 minutes to hit the ground.
Named after the Greek personification of dread, twin of Phobos (fear).

bodies.name: Io
facts: The most volcanically active body in the solar system, with hundreds of active volcanoes.
Squeezed by Jupiter's immense tidal gravity, which flexes its interior and generates the heat driving that volcanism.
One of the four Galilean moons discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610.

bodies.name: Europa
facts: Its icy shell likely hides a liquid water ocean with more water than all of Earth's oceans combined.
One of the most promising places in the solar system to search for extraterrestrial life.
Has one of the smoothest surfaces of any known solid body, criss-crossed by long cracks.

bodies.name: Ganymede
facts: The largest moon in the solar system — bigger than the planet Mercury.
The only moon known to generate its own magnetic field.
Believed to have a saltwater ocean sandwiched between layers of ice.

bodies.name: Callisto
facts: The most heavily cratered object in the solar system, with a surface unchanged for billions of years.
Orbits far enough from Jupiter to receive much less radiation than the inner Galilean moons.
Likely has a small liquid saltwater layer deep beneath its icy crust.

bodies.name: Mimas
facts: Its enormous Herschel crater, a third of Mimas's own diameter, gives it a striking resemblance to the Death Star.
The smallest astronomical body known to be rounded by its own gravity.
Orbits within Saturn's E ring, inside the planet's Roche limit for icy material.

bodies.name: Enceladus
facts: Geysers at its south pole blast water-ice plumes into space, feeding Saturn's E ring.
One of the most reflective objects in the solar system because its surface is almost pure ice.
Has a subsurface global ocean and is a leading candidate for hosting microbial life.

bodies.name: Tethys
facts: Home to Ithaca Chasma, a canyon system stretching most of the way around the moon.
Made almost entirely of water ice, giving it a very low density.
Shares its orbit with two small Trojan moons, Telesto and Calypso.

bodies.name: Dione
facts: Bright wispy streaks on its trailing hemisphere turned out to be tectonic ice cliffs, not frost deposits as first thought.
Has faint, dusty rings of its own — the first found around a moon.
Denser than most other icy Saturnian moons, suggesting a larger rocky core.

bodies.name: Rhea
facts: Saturn's second-largest moon, made mostly of water ice with a small rocky core.
May have a thin oxygen and carbon dioxide atmosphere, extremely rare for a moon.
Once suspected to have its own ring system, though later observations found no direct evidence.

bodies.name: Titan
facts: The only moon in the solar system with a substantial atmosphere, thicker than Earth's.
Has stable lakes and rivers of liquid methane and ethane on its surface — the only other body known to have liquid on its surface.
Larger than the planet Mercury, and the second-largest moon in the solar system after Ganymede.

bodies.name: Iapetus
facts: Famously two-toned: one hemisphere is as dark as coal, the other as bright as snow.
Has a strange equatorial ridge up to 20km high, giving it a walnut-like shape.
Orbits much farther from Saturn than its other major moons, tilted 15° from Saturn's equatorial plane.

bodies.name: Miranda
facts: Has some of the tallest known cliffs in the solar system, including Verona Rupes at up to 20km high.
Its jumbled, patchwork surface suggests it may have been shattered and reassembled by an ancient impact.
The innermost and smallest of Uranus's five major moons.

bodies.name: Ariel
facts: The brightest of Uranus's major moons, with a relatively young, lightly cratered surface.
Criss-crossed by deep canyons far larger than anything similar on Earth relative to its size.
Named after a spirit in Alexander Pope's poem 'The Rape of the Lock', continuing Uranus's literary naming theme.

bodies.name: Umbriel
facts: The darkest of Uranus's major moons, reflecting only about 16% of the sunlight that hits it.
Features a mysterious bright ring-shaped feature nicknamed 'the fluorescent Cheerio'.
Named after a dusky spirit from 'The Rape of the Lock', fitting its dark surface.

bodies.name: Titania
facts: The largest moon of Uranus, with a surface scarred by huge canyons and fault valleys.
May harbor a thin layer of liquid water between its icy mantle and rocky core.
Named after the queen of the fairies in Shakespeare's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'.

bodies.name: Oberon
facts: The outermost of Uranus's five major moons, heavily cratered with a reddish tint on its trailing hemisphere.
Has a mountain near its south pole rising about 11km high, visible on its horizon in Voyager 2 images.
Named after the king of the fairies, opposite Titania, in Shakespeare's 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'.

bodies.name: Triton
facts: The only large moon in the solar system that orbits its planet backwards (retrograde), suggesting it's a captured Kuiper Belt object.
Has active nitrogen geysers, making it one of the few geologically active moons.
Its retrograde orbit is slowly decaying — in a few billion years, tidal forces will tear it apart, likely forming a ring around Neptune.

bodies.name: Ceres
facts: The largest object in the asteroid belt and the only dwarf planet located in the inner solar system.
Contains roughly a third of the asteroid belt's total mass, despite being just under 950km across.
NASA's Dawn spacecraft found bright salt deposits and evidence of a subsurface ocean of brine.

bodies.name: Pluto
facts: Reclassified from the ninth planet to a dwarf planet in 2006 after the discovery of similarly-sized Kuiper Belt objects.
Its orbit is so eccentric and tilted that it was closer to the Sun than Neptune from 1979 to 1999.
Its largest moon, Charon, is more than half Pluto's size — the two are sometimes called a double dwarf planet.

bodies.name: Halley's Comet
facts: The most famous comet, visible from Earth roughly every 76 years — last seen in 1986, due back in 2061.
Its 162° orbital inclination means it travels retrograde and steeply tilted relative to the planets.
Its glowing tail always points away from the Sun, pushed back by solar wind and radiation pressure — not trailing behind its motion.

bodies.name: Comet Encke
facts: Has the shortest orbital period of any known comet — just 3.3 years.
Its frequent close solar passes have boiled away its surface ices, giving it one of the darkest surfaces of any comet.
The Taurid meteor showers on Earth are debris shed from Encke's orbital trail.
